extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers learning to evaluate or construct philosophical and logical arguments (critical thinkers in philosophy/science)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual tests for identifying and classifying fallacies in argumentative reasoning, with guidance on how errors arise (false evidence, inconclusive evidence, suppressed premises, a priori assumptions) and how to expose them. Aimed at improving critical evaluation of inductive and deductive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fivefold classification of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments' errors can be usefully classified into five classes (Fallacies of Observation, Fallacies of Generalization, Fallacies of Confusion, Fallacies of Ratiocination, and Fallacies of Simple Inspection/_a priori_).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to locate the 'seat' of error in an argument, but be aware that many real-world errors run into each other and an individual fallacy may plausibly be assigned to more than one class. When an argument is fully stated with all steps explicit, an erroneous argument will clearly fall into one of these modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies where the facts on which induction proceeds are erroneous (malobservation, non-observation, or mistaken inference about observed marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as failures in ascertaining the facts on which a theory is grounded; includes both direct bad observation and errors produced by intermediate marks that do not prove what they are supposed to prove. Check the factual basis and whether observations genuinely support claimed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies in which the facts are correct but the conclusion is not warranted by them (over-generalization from limited or inappropriate evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the induction unjustifiably extends from observed instances to wider claims; consider subordinate forms (e.g., hasty generalization, false causal inference) and test whether the available evidence actually bears out the claimed general conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive fallacies in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion—cases of vicious argumentation guarded against by syllogistic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the logical relation between premises and conclusion (distribution of terms, validity of syllogistic steps). Even with true premises, check whether they logically support the conclusion or whether the argument is an unsound syllogism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from neglect or inability to state the question properly and to apprehend the evidence with definiteness and precision (includes reasoning in a circle and other confusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the error is primarily one of conceptual confusion—lack of distinct conception of premises or question—rather than false facts or invalid syllogistic form. Many fallacies may be ultimately classed here when confusion is the dominant characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressed premise detection (filling tacit links)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many arguments omit one or more tacit premises; to detect fallacy, the silently assumed proposition must be supplied and tested for truth or for whether it proves the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a link is suppressed, attempt to supply the missing premise(s). Judge whether the supplied premise is (a) not true (which would make it a fallacy of observation/generalization) or (b) true but does not prove the conclusion (a fallacy of ratiocination). Be aware that different hearers may supply different suppressed premises leading to different classifications of the fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mixed/clustered fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies often 'herd or cluster together'—one fallacy (e.g., malobservation) can facilitate or convert into another (e.g., false generalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume neat exclusivity of types in practice; trace causal chains (how one error predisposed another) and identify the most probable seat of error given human tendencies and the nature of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori (Simple Inspection) fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors where propositions are embraced as self-evident or requiring no proof; the mind assumes that certain truths can be known by inspection without empirical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims presented as needing no proof. The text warns that deciding which propositions legitimately require no proof is a deep metaphysical problem; practically, look for unwarranted reliance on 'intuition' or assumed self-evidence and request empirical or inferential support where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking subjective ideas for objective reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that what is true of our ideas or the order of our thoughts must be true of external objects (e.g., if we always think two things together they must always exist together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether a claimed relation is a feature of mental association rather than an objective relation among things; avoid deriving ontology from mere conceptual or imaginative associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of abstractions (reification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity to treat names of abstractions (e.g., Nature, Fate, Whiteness) as denoting distinct objective entities (Substantiae Secundae) rather than convenient ways of speaking about collections of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question whether a general term names an independently existing entity or merely abstracts common features of particulars. Reject unwarranted ontological commitments that arise solely from linguistic or conceptual convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from inconceivability (what is inconceivable must be false)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy of concluding that something cannot be true because it cannot be conceived (e.g., antipodes thought impossible; early objections to Copernican system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not declare propositions false merely because they are difficult or currently impossible for us to conceive; limits of imagination or present experience do not establish impossibility in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to 'what is easily conceivable' as a guide to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the explanation which can be conceived most easily (or is simplest) is likeliest to be true ('nature always acts by the simplest means').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid privileging hypotheses because they seem simpler or more imaginable; historical examples (e.g., celestial spheres) show that apparent simplicity can be misleading and may require ever-increasing complication to fit facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of Sufficient Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that because we see no reason for a phenomenon to deviate in a particular way, it therefore will not deviate (e.g., inferring persistence of rest because there is no reason for motion in a particular direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of asserting that lack of an identified sufficient reason entails impossibility of change; this may covertly assume the very principle requiring proof (petitio principii). Demand empirical or independent theoretical justification rather than reasoning from absence-of-reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: fully state and make explicit all steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sophistry can be constrained to throw its sophistry into distinct form (all steps stated explicitly), it often requires no further exposure; a fully stated erroneous argument will be clearly one of the classified fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical method for peer review or critique, require authors to state all premises and inferential steps explicitly; this exposes suppressed premises and clarifies whether the error is factual, inferential, or conceptual.
